newsitem.title: MALAWI: Malawi economy recovers, still fragile - World Bank.
newsitem.headline: Malawi economy recovers, still fragile - World Bank.

text.p: Malawi's economy shows signs of improvement, with a sharp drop in inflation and interest rates this year and some boost in trade, according to the World Bank.
But the Bank's latest report on this southern African country says it is too early to tell whether this is the beginning of a sustained growth phase.

"While there are some signs of recovery in the real economy from the sluggishness of the past two years, it is still too early to tell whether this is the beginning of a sustained spurt of growth," the Bank said in a report released this week.

Interest rates charged by commercial banks have dropped to 29 percent from 46 percent while annual consumer price inflation rate has fallen 10 percentage points, to 21.5 percent in September, the latest data available.
Underlying the better outlook has been a sharp increase in the maize crop, with the 1996 harvest 30 percent above normal at 1.8 million tonnes, following good rains.

The Bank said exports in the first half of the fiscal year, from April to September, were estimated 32 percent higher at 2,506 million kwacha ($167 million) compared to 1,900 million in the same period last year.
Imports are put at 4,239 million compared to 3,245 million.
Foreign exchange reserves have also risen substantially and are currently equivalent to six months of import cover.
But the Bank cautioned the government needed to keep strict controls of expenditure.
"Some ministries have already spent their budget allocation for the whole year," World Bank Representative in Malawi Arif Zulfiquar told Reuters.
Total expenditure for April-September was 4.4 billion kwacha, representing just over 50 percent of the budget for the whole year.

"The fiscal situation has improved since the first part of the year. However, the situation remains tight -- strict control will need to be maintained over expenditures and many ministries could face a squeeze during the rest of the financial year," the report said.
